pending_items.title: Libya’s Haftar visits old foe Turkey in a first, hails ‘new phase’ of ties
pending_items.content:
Khalifa Haftar, leader of the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls the eastern coast of the North African nation, arrived in Ankara Wednesday on his first official visit to Turkey.

Haftar arrived in Turkey with a delegation including his son and presumed heir, Saddam Haftar, as ties between the two old foes begin to thaw.

While Haftar controls eastern Libya, Turkey backed the UN-recognised government based in the capital Tripoli in western Libya during the civil war. In recent years, however, has sought to deepen ties with power brokers across the divided country.

Haftar met with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and other senior Turkish officials in Ankara on Wednesday.

The talks marked "an important step" in building trust and "laid the groundwork for a new phase in relations" between the eastern half of divided Libya and Turkey, said Saddam Haftar in a Facebook post.

Read more Haftar’s sons rise in Libya’s east, bringing ‘corruption, death, destruction’

Erdogan's office did not provide details of the closed-door talks. Video footage showed the two leaders exchanging a warm handshake.

Earlier, Haftar met Turkey's foreign and energy ministers, intelligence chief and military leaders, according to images shared by the foreign ministry.

The talks focused on the latest regional and international developments, as well as issues of mutual interest, a statement from Haftar's office said.

"Both sides also explored ways to strengthen cooperation between Libya and Turkey across several sectors in a manner that serves the shared interests of both countries," the statement said.

Libya has been wracked by unrest since the 2011 uprising that toppled and killed longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi.

Turkey intervened in support of the Tripoli government when it came under siege from Haftar's forces, supplying armed drones that helped repel an offensive on the capital in 2019.

In 2020, Erdogan described Haftar as "a mercenary" and accused regional powers including the United Arab Emirates and Egypt of funding him.

But Ankara has since repaired ties with several regional actors and expanded contacts with eastern Libyan authorities as part of efforts to bridge the country's political divide.

Haftar's son Saddam said earlier on social media that he had visited Qatar, another regional player involved in mediation efforts.

Turkey hosted talks in October between representatives of Haftar's administration and the rival government in Tripoli, and remains one of the few countries maintaining ties with both camps.

Erdogan met Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah of Libya's Tripoli-based government on November 12 on the sidelines of the climate summit in the southern resort of Antalya.

The trip by Haftar comes three days after a Ukrainian attack on two Russian ships near the eastern Libyan city of Benghazi.

Read more Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone at Benghazi naval base

Ukraine said the attacks on Sunday caused the Russian corvette Merkury to explode and sink at the port of Benghazi, while a dry cargo vessel was also hit.

Ukraine, which claimed responsibility for the two attacks, alleged Russia was transporting weapons.

The incident has raised fears of a deepening crisis in Libya.

The Tripoli government has sought clarification from Ukraine, while the eastern authorities have called for an international investigation into allegations of a Ukrainian military presence in Libya.

Haftar maintains close ties with Russia, while Turkey has sought to mediate between Moscow and Kyiv since the start of the Ukraine war.

In October, Libya's eastern-based parliament approved a contested maritime boundaries agreement signed with Turkey in 2019, drawing criticism from the European Union and several eastern Mediterranean states.

pending_items.title: US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year
pending_items.content:
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has undercut US President Donald Trump's assertion earlier this month that he "won't be paying Israel" by the end of this year.

Huckabee, the former governor of Arkansas who is an evangelical pastor and a staunch Zionist - by his own description - said on Tuesday at a conference in Tel Aviv that he's " not certain that there will be a cessation on an abrupt basis by the end of this year".

That's because Washington currently gives Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028.

The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes.

In May, the Israeli defence ministry said that the two sides had begun formal talks to replace the current memorandum, with discussions focusing on joint investment in research, development and weapons production.

The suggested framework was to move the relationship from aid to a more reciprocal partnership.

The Congressional Research Service, a non-partisan research body that advises the US Congress, further confirmed this in a June report that US and Israeli officials were discussing a possible shift after 2028 away from direct military aid and towards joint programmes.

In July, the Republican-controlled House of Representatives narrowly passed a $1.5 trillion budget for the US Department of War, and the bill included a controversial provision that would permanently integrate US and Israeli military tech advancements in a way that would - as Netanyahu put it - turn Israel from a foreign aid recipient to a full-scale partner.

Future presidents would not be able to simply withdraw from such a project.

The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is must-pass legislation, as it is needed to fund all of the Pentagon's operations in the year to come. The Senate will have to consider it soon.

But emboldened by the incoming Democratic majority in January, a dozen Democrats, led by Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen , are seeking to remove the provisions related to Section 219, which establishes the "United States–Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative".

The project would identify jointly developed or Israeli-origin technologies for potential integration into US systems; ensure collaborative research initiatives involving government, private sector and academic institutions in both countries protect "sensitive technology"; and ultimately align military efforts with the Department of War that include the Irregular Warfare Technical Support Directorate, the Defense Innovation Unit, the Missile Defense Agency and the United States Space Command, among others.

Huckabee said at the Institute for National Security Studies conference on Tuesday that American lives are saved "every day" because "we pick up intelligence from our partners in Israel".

On 3 November, Trump said that his administration will not give its yearly military aid to Israel starting next year, because of a prior understanding he made with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Trump added that weapon sales and other forms of military cooperation would continue.

Speaking on Fox News, the president said that the two had agreed months ago to end the military aid since Israel no longer needed it.

“Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4bn a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping,” Trump said.

“We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it,” he added.

Trump said Israel would be able to purchase weapons from the United States and other countries, suggesting that the change would affect the form of assistance rather than bring an end to military ties.

"They can buy whatever they want. They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world," he said. The comments came as Republican lawmakers and establishment Democrats running for Congress - as well as hundreds of statewide races - faced growing electoral pressure over support for Israel ahead of the midterm elections.

And indeed, the so-called blue tsunami , led by an energised progressive Democratic movement that wants to curb US aid to Israel, washed over Capitol Hill and state legislatures, including several governorships.

pending_items.title: Israeli judges recommend prosecutors drop one bribery case against Netanyahu
pending_items.content:
JERUSALEM, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Israeli judges on Wednesday recommended that prosecutors drop one of three long-running cases against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and reconsider another alleging he granted favours in exchange for positive media coverage.

Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust. He denies the charges and has pleaded not guilty. His trial began in 2020 and involves three criminal cases.

In the case referred to as Case 4000, prosecutors allege that Netanyahu granted regulatory favours worth around 1.8 billion shekels (about $500 million) to Bezeq Telecom Israel. In return, prosecutors say, he sought positive coverage for himself and his wife, Sara, on a news website controlled by former Bezeq Chairman Shaul Elovitch. Elovitch has denied wrongdoing.

In a blow to prosecutors, Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman of Jerusalem District Court, who presides over Case 4000, told Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara at a hearing on Wednesday that a conviction was unlikely and the case should be dropped.

The recommendation was not a ruling on the case, the court clarified, and Baharav-Miara said she would review the court's statements with the prosecution.

The judges also recommended prosecutors reconsider so-called Case 2000 because of doubts that Netanyahu's actions constituted a criminal offense. In that case, prosecutors allege Netanyahu negotiated a deal with Arnon Mozes, owner of Israel's Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper, for better coverage in return for legislation to slow the growth of a rival newspaper.

Netanyahu on Wednesday called the court's recommendation a "ray of light for truth and justice."

"Ten years of suffering for dozens of my close ones who were dragged into interrogation rooms," Netanyahu said in a televised address. "Where they were blackmailed with criminal acts, humiliated, and the lives of many of them were ruined, just so they would give false testimony against me."

(Reporting by Emily Rose; Editing by Cynthia Osterman)

pending_items.title: Netanyahu says corruption trial ‘must end’ as court suggests dropping case
pending_items.content:
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for an immediate end to his long-running corruption trial after judges cast doubt on the charges and recommended dropping a case in which he is accused of bribery.

Netanyahu on Wednesday said the “fabricated cases” against him were falling apart, in a televised statement at the Israeli parliament.

The judges’ recommendations came as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival after inconclusive October 27 elections.

Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot , has been tasked with forming a government, and if Netanyahu is no longer prime minister, he would lose his leverage to avoid a potential jail sentence.

“Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family,” Netanyahu said in his speech.

“Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul. Who will give those years back to us?”

“The trial must end immediately,” he added.

During a hearing in Jerusalem on Wednesday regarding three corruption cases against Netanyahu, judges recommended dropping one, reconsidering another and suggested resolving the third through an agreement, Israeli media reported.

In Case 4000, in which Netanyahu is accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, judges indicated there was little chance of a conviction.

That case is considered to be the most serious Netanyahu faces and involves him allegedly offering regulatory favours for a telecoms company in exchange for favourable media coverage.

Netanyahu is alleged to have negotiated with Shaul Elovitch, the controlling shareholder of Israeli telecommunications giant Bezeq, to get positive coverage on his Walla news site in exchange for policies benefitting Bezeq.

On Wednesday, Israeli media reported Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman saying that proving the bribery charge in that case faced “considerable difficulties”.

Netanyahu, who has been in power on and off for three decades, has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and denounced the cases as a politically motivated plot against him.

He is the first sitting Israeli prime minister to stand trial.

Israel’s Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who was unusually summoned to the hearing on Wednesday, said she would consider the judges’ recommendations and was ready for either a verdict or a plea deal.

In Case 2000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over an alleged deal with the owner of Yediot Aharonot for favourable coverage in exchange for curbs on rival newspaper Israel Hayom. Judges on Wednesday questioned whether his actions constituted a crime and recommended reconsidering the case.

In Case 1000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over allegedly accepting luxury gifts from wealthy individuals in exchange for favours. Judges recommended reaching an agreement to conclude the case.

Netanyahu’s right-wing allies cheered the court’s recommendations and demanded the trial be brought to an end.

“After years of persecution against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the time has come to put an end to a trial that was flawed from the outset,” Israel Katz, who is the defence minister in Netanyahu’s caretaker government, wrote on X.

Netanyahu’s corruption trial opened in May 2020.

During his most recent term, which started in late 2022, Netanyahu proposed far-reaching judicial reforms that critics say sought to weaken the courts.

With coalition negotiations under way, Eisenkot’s camp is already trying to start unravelling some of the Netanyahu-era judicial reforms in parliament.

The presidential contender is expected to meet Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday evening.

His centrist Yashar party said a day earlier that it had agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.

Lieberman has ruled out forming a coalition with Arab-led parties that could hand them a majority in parliament. That has frustrated Democrats chief Yair Golan, who has been pushing Eisenkot to reach a deal with parties representing Israel’s 21 percent Arab minority to make good on his campaign promise to bring down Netanyahu.

Eisenkot also faced a new challenge on Tuesday after the left-wing Democrats suspended coalition talks, further complicating his potential path to power.

The Yashar party leader has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.
